titre: One Stray Rivet Proves Nothing; Five Rivets in Place Outline a Ship
accroche: At Sutton Hoo, in May 1939, Basil Brown follows five rivets left in place to a ship. In 1938, scattered rivets did not at once suggest a ship.
contenu_vulgarise:
A rusty iron rivet is only a piece of metal. Everything depends on where it is found, and on what surrounds it.

## 1938: rivets that don't at once suggest a ship

At Sutton Hoo, in Suffolk, the owner of the estate, Edith Pretty, hires the local archaeologist Basil Brown in 1938. In June and July he opens three mounds (mounds 2, 3, and 4). Tomb robbers had been there before him. In mound 2, Brown recognizes pieces of iron for what they are, ship rivets. But the robbers had scattered them, and these fragments did not at once suggest a ship burial. There was one, nonetheless: according to the Sutton Hoo Society, mound 2 held a ship, the second of its kind found in England. Mounds 3 and 4, cremation burials, yielded fragments of objects from afar, and the Sutton Hoo Society notes that the site's wealth and contacts reached as far as the eastern Mediterranean.

## 1939: five rivets in place

In May 1939, Brown returns to mound 1, the largest. He stops at the first piece of iron he meets and finds five, still in position, on what turns out to be a ship's prow. He widens the trench to follow the shape that is appearing: planks, ribs, thole pins.

Between one isolated rivet and five rivets in place, the difference is one of kind. A displaced object tells you about its material. Objects left in place tell you about the structure they held, because their relative positions preserve a pattern. That pattern is what makes it possible to recognize a ship.

On June 14, 1939, Brown reaches the burial chamber, at the center of the ship. A medieval quarry had altered the shape of the mound: the robbers had dug in the wrong place and missed the chamber.

## The handoff

When the intact state of the chamber becomes apparent, Edith Pretty judges that specialists are needed. The excavation passes to Charles Phillips, of the University of Cambridge, and his team. In seventeen days, they remove 263 objects from the chamber. Phillips identifies the burials as Anglo-Saxon rather than Viking, which, the National Trust notes, confirms Brown's conclusion.

The story therefore does not rest on the contrast of an amateur and experts. It rests on an inference: an excavator who stops at the first iron and widens his trench to follow the shape that appears. Rivets of the same kind, displaced by the robbers, did not at once suggest a ship a year earlier.

One question remains, which every excavation deposit raises: how many objects, removed from their position, have lost what they would have said in place?

repere.texte: Once the excavation is entrusted to Charles Phillips, of the University of Cambridge, his team removes 263 objects from the burial chamber of Sutton Hoo mound 1 in seventeen days.

carte.punch: Scattered, rivets don't at once suggest a ship. Five rivets in place outline one.
carte.idee: At Sutton Hoo, iron rivets scattered by robbers did not at once suggest a ship in 1938. In May 1939, Basil Brown finds five still in place on a prow: he follows the shape and reaches the burial chamber on June 14.

quiz.question: Why didn't the rivets in mound 2, in 1938, at once suggest a ship, unlike those of 1939?
choix: Those of 1938 were too corroded for Brown to identify them as rivets
Brown did not yet have permission to excavate mound 2 in 1938
Scattered by the robbers, they did not at once suggest a ship; those of 1939 were in position
Those of 1938 came from a cremation burial, unrelated to a ship
quiz.explication: In 1938, Brown already recognized ship rivets, but the robbers had scattered them and they did not at once suggest a ship burial. In 1939, five rivets left in position on the prow provided a pattern to follow. Neither the condition of the pieces, nor the permission to excavate, nor the nature of the burial explains the difference.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the robbers miss the burial chamber of mound 1?
choix: A medieval quarry had altered the shape of the mound, hence digging in the wrong place
The chamber was closed by a stone slab they could not lift
They never tried to dig into this mound, judged too large
The whole ship had been moved a few meters after they came through
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the National Trust, the old quarry had changed the appearance of the mound and the robbers dug somewhere other than over the chamber, which remained intact. Nothing indicates a sealed slab, an absence of digging, or a displacement of the ship.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who takes over the excavation once the chamber is reached?
choix: A British Army team, stationed on site to protect it
Edith Pretty herself, with the staff of her estate
A University of Cambridge team assembled by Charles Phillips
An American museum mission, at the owner's invitation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Edith Pretty judges that specialists are needed: the excavation passes to Charles Phillips, of the University of Cambridge, and his team, who remove 263 objects in seventeen days.
